This document collects supporting analyses for the main text. Section references, metric names (PC1, PC2, ΔMMR) and methods follow the main paper.

1 Per-server data summary

The corpus is 92.7 million ranked games from the top ~1,000 players on each of eight regional servers. Servers differ by an order of magnitude in game volume, from 2.3 million games on OC1 to 30.1 million on EUW1 (Table S 1). They also differ sharply in how many players carry an individually significant circadian phase: JP1 is an extreme outlier, with roughly three quarters of its players reaching the Benjamini–Hochberg threshold on both behavioural components, against 10–28% everywhere else. This is a symptom of JP1’s daily maintenance shutdown (~05:00–11:00 local; main-text Figure 1): the truncated sampling window makes the fitted 24 h sinusoid look artificially strong and places its peak in unsampled hours. We therefore exclude JP1 from all phase-based analyses (the FDR fractions, the modality fits and the kernel density); it is retained only in the period analysis and the play-volume figure. The per-server row for JP1 below is shown for completeness and is flagged accordingly.

2 Within-subject rhythm summary

Each server’s within-subject periodogram peaks within a few minutes of 24.0 h for both behavioural components and for ΔMMR (Figure S 1, left; JP1’s two flagged harmonic peaks are the outliers screened from the period meta-analysis): the circadian period is not a pooled artefact but recurs server by server, with the N-weighted mean sitting on 24 h. The fraction of players carrying an individually significant phase separates behaviour from success (Figure S 1, right; JP1 excluded): 14.2% of players for PC1 and 10.3% for PC2, against 0.3% for ΔMMR. Skill change has almost no per-player circadian signal, which is why it cannot be tested for modality.

3 Phase variation is not inherited from the play-time schedule

The wide individual spread of behavioural peak phases (main text) is not an echo of when people play. A natural worry is that the behavioural phases only reproduce the shape of the play-time schedule. We tested this directly. For each analysed player we took the circular-mean hour of their games in local time — their preferred play time — and pooled these across servers (7,966 players), then described the distribution with the same circular fits used for the behavioural phases. This complements Figure 1 of the main text, which makes the point at the level of the server: aggregate play volume follows a single evening-peaked curve on every server once local time is used. Here we ask about individual players.

The preferred-play-time distribution is single-peaked and comparatively tight (Figure S 2, Table S 2): it concentrates in the evening around 19.6 h with a concentration of \(\kappa \approx 2.6\) (circular standard deviation ≈ 3 h), and BIC prefers one component over two (ΔBIC = 1.8 in favour of the single component). The behavioural peak phases, by contrast, are single-moded but spread more than twice as widely (circular standard deviation ≈ 7 h; main text ?@sec-bimodality). Players cluster their log-on times into the evening far more tightly than their behaviour peaks, so the broad individual variation in behavioural phase is a property of how players behave at a given hour, not of the hours they choose to play.
